candidates.attacker_control: Remote, unauthenticated HTTP client: it controls the HTTP request method and the Authorization header (it can simply omit the header or supply bad credentials). No prior access to the server is needed.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the GET clause could be an intentional 'public WSDL/GET' feature: no comment or configuration flag indicates that, and it applies to the JAX-RS registry as well as the WSDL registry, so it silently overrides the operator's auth=BASIC choice. Checked for a second copy of the wrapper elsewhere (only two call sites). Checked that Tomcat-based deployments (TomcatRsRegistry) ignore `auth` and therefore are unaffected. Checked that the failure branch really is empty (no sendError/401). Could not verify downstream role enforcement for CXF/EJB-backed resources; for EJB-backed resources with @RolesAllowed the container's own identity check may still deny the unauthenticated call, but POJO/JAX-RS resources have no additional gate in-server.
candidates.impact: Defeats an explicitly configured access-control control: any client can invoke GET operations of JAX-RS/JAX-WS endpoints deployed through these registries without credentials (unauthorized data retrieval / method invocation). Failed POST/PUT/DELETE logins also leak no 401 challenge, which can mislead clients into thinking a call succeeded.
candidates.prerequisites: The EJB/HTTP server is running the standalone/embedded OpenEJB REST or Web-Service service (org.apache.openejb.server.rest.RESTService / openejb-webservices) and the operator has explicitly configured BASIC auth (`auth=BASIC` service property for RESTService.init, or authMethod=BASIC for OpenEJBHttpWsRegistry) — i.e. the deployment asked for authentication. Tomcat-managed TomEE does not use this wrapper (tomee-jaxrs/TomcatRsRegistry ignores `auth` and relies on Tomcat constraints), which limits the affected deployment mode.
candidates.root_cause: BasicAuthHttpListenerWrapper.onMessage only fails closed for non-GET methods: the guard is `if (token != null || HttpRequest.Method.GET.name().equals(request.getMethod())) { httpListener.onMessage(...); }`. When the Authorization header is missing, malformed, or the credentials fail, `token` stays null but the wrapped listener is still invoked for every GET; the else branch is empty even though the comment says "login failed, return 401", so non-GET failures also return no 401. The wrapper is the only authentication gate for the standalone/embedded registries that use it.
candidates.title: BASIC authentication wrapper executes GET requests without credentials (auth bypass in openejb-http)
candidates.trace: HTTP request -> HttpListenerRegistry.onMessage matches the deployed REST/WS regex and calls the ClassLoaderHttpListener -> BasicAuthHttpListenerWrapper.onMessage: 'Authorization' absent/unparseable -> token stays null; however method == GET satisfies `token != null || GET` -> wrapped RsHttpListener/JAX-WS listener.onMessage(request, response) is executed (securityService.associate/disassociate are skipped). Non-GET requests fall into the empty else branch and are silently dropped without setting 401.
candidates.unverified: Whether any production distribution enables these openejb-rest/openejb-webservices services with auth=BASIC by default (the default is `auth=NONE`), and whether downstream CXF/JAX-RS code performs an independent role check for every affected endpoint; the wrapper is also reachable through async dispatch paths that were not exhaustively reviewed.

coverage_summary: Scope: 4,278 model-visible files (all source files present in the snapshot; no src/test trees except a single test file, no binaries). The P1 relation index reports complete indexing of all 4,278 files (no missing/unparsed files), 44,218 symbols / 107,193 calls / 73,428 edges / 1,097 facts, but provides only syntactic navigation hints (no data-flow, reachability or scanner findings), and I verified index hints against source text. I read in depth: server/openejb-ejbd (EjbDaemon protocol), server/openejb-client (Client, EjbObjectInputStream, JNDI), server/openejb-http (HttpListenerRegistry, HttpRequestImpl, BasicAuthHttpListenerWrapper, ServerServlet, sessions), server/openejb-rest + openejb-webservices (registry wrapping), server/openejb-hessian, server/openejb-ssh + openejb-common-cli (PathCommand/CatCommand/PartCommand/ScriptFileCommand/CliRunnable), server/openejb-server (ServiceDaemon), container/openejb-core (ivm EjbObjectInputStream/BaseEjbProxyHandler, ObjectInputStreamFiltered, QuartzObjectInputStream, core/security jaas+jacc+AbstractSecurityService, ObjectInputStreamFiltered, timer/TimerData, util/PojoSerialization, ProvisioningClassLoaderConfigurer, cipher package, config/DeploymentLoader), tomee/tomee-catalina (TomcatWebAppBuilder, OpenEJBContextConfig, realm classes, valves, EmbeddedServletContext-related code), tomee/tomee-common (installer), tomee-webapp/tomee-webaccess (web.xml constraints, InstallerServlet), tomee-embedded (Container), tomee-loader, maven/tomee-maven-plugin, examples/polling and moviefun samples. I did not exhaustively review the generated JAXB model code (container/openejb-jee), the very large generated TomEETldScanner, most example applications, the OSGi/TCK modules, or all ~1,000 files of container/openejb-core line by line.
limitations: No code was compiled, executed, or tested; no runtime confirmation of any finding is claimed.
The P1 index is syntactic only (no taint/data-flow/reachability proof), and its facts/edges were used solely for navigation and then checked against source text.

Dependencies that determine exploitability are external to the snapshot (OpenWebBeans MockServletContext used by EmbeddedServletContext, Tomcat 8.0.32 servlet constraints, CXF/JAX-RS role enforcement, JAAS configuration files, Hessian library), so their behaviour could not be verified locally.

No upstream repository, release tags, patches, CVE data or previous outputs were consulted, so I could not diff this snapshot against the corresponding upstream revision to distinguish genuine upstream code from any modified/injected code; conclusions are limited to what the snapshot text shows.

Several findings depend on non-default configuration (auth=BASIC for the selected candidate; openejb.embedded.http.resources for the resource-serving traversal; openejb-ssh for the CLI traversal), so real-world exposure may be limited to those deployment modes.

The selected candidate is a lead with low confidence: the GET-permitting clause could conceivably be a deliberate product decision, and downstream role checks for some resource types might still reject unauthenticated calls.

rejected_leads.lead: CVE-2016-0779-style Java deserialization RCE in EjbObjectInputStream (container/openejb-core .../core/ivm/EjbObjectInputStream.java, server/openejb-client .../client/EjbObjectInputStream.java, core/rmi/BlacklistClassResolver.java)
rejected_leads.reason: The historic vulnerable state is already mitigated in this snapshot: both streams call BlacklistClassResolver.DEFAULT.check()/the nested resolver before loading, ObjectInputStreamFiltered and QuartzObjectInputStream are also filtered, and the EJB protocol streams are the hardened subclasses. The residual weakness (only four prefix entries, and resolveProxyClass performs no blacklist check) reads as incomplete hardening/defense-in-depth rather than an unmitigated vulnerability, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal / arbitrary file read in embedded resource serving (server/openejb-http .../HttpListenerRegistry.java:193-214 `new File(f, pathWithoutSlash)`)
rejected_leads.reason: The path is taken from the decoded request URI (`getServletPath()` -> `uri.getPath()`) and contains no '..' filtering, but the file-serving branch only runs when `openejb.embedded.http.resources` is configured (set by test tooling such as ApplicationComposers/@WebResource); with the default empty resourceBases the request falls through to ServletContext.getResource(), whose behavior depends on the external OpenWebBeans MockServletContext and could not be verified from this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: CLI path-restriction bypass in server/openejb-common-cli (.../command/PathCommand.java:27-43, plus ScriptFileCommand.java:35 which never calls resolve())
rejected_leads.reason: `path.startsWith("..")` does not catch embedded '..' segments (e.g. `x/../../../../etc/passwd`, or `$base/../../etc/passwd`) so the 'in tomee directories only' contract can be escaped for cat/ls/part, and `script file <path>` reads/executes an arbitrary file. However this requires access to the optional openejb-ssh CLI with valid JAAS credentials, and for authenticated CLI users the `script` command already permits arbitrary script/code execution, so the incremental impact is low.

rejected_leads.lead: Auto-created default admin credentials (tomee/tomee) in TomcatWebAppBuilder.start(StandardServer) lines 415-437, installer/Installer.java line 150, tomee-webaccess conf/tomcat-users.xml)
rejected_leads.reason: Real source evidence of hard-coded default credentials granted the tomee-admin role (which gates the /tomee installer, ServerServlet remote EJB/JNDI, and webaccess webapp), but this is documented/intended TomEE behaviour for the default profile when no users exist, not a control that fails, so it was treated as a configuration weakness rather than the selected vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: InstallerServlet parameter handling and JSON escaping (tomee/tomee-webapp .../InstallerServlet.java:35-79)
rejected_leads.reason: The `!= null && "".equals(trim())` conditions only apply empty values, so request parameters never influence the installer paths (this actually removes attacker control); the escape() order bug (quotes escaped before backslashes) can corrupt JSON but the values are server-side paths/messages, not attacker-controlled, so no concrete injection was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip extraction without canonical-path checks (container/openejb-loader .../Zips.java, arquillian/.../common/Zips.java)
rejected_leads.reason: Missing zip-slip validation exists, but the archives are locally provided TomEE/test artifacts; an attacker would first need to supply the archive, so no reachable trust boundary was substantiated.

rejected_leads.lead: Weak TLS defaults (ServiceDaemon.java:130 and SocketConnectionFactory.java:91 default enabledCipherSuites `SSL_DH_anon_WITH_RC4_128_MD5`)
rejected_leads.reason: Only applied when the optional `secure` mode is enabled and not explicitly configured; legacy upstream default rather than a reachable defect in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Predictable session IDs via QuickSessionManager/FastNonSecureRandom (tomee-catalina/session, tomee-embedded)
rejected_leads.reason: Explicitly opt-in 'quick/insecure' performance mode for tests and embedded use; not enabled by the default configuration.

Potentially allows authentication when both the stored DB password and the client-supplied password are null, but requires a NULL password column and a custom client that sends a null credential; the code is upstream-style and the exploit conditions are narrow, so it was not selected over the auth-wrapper bypass.

summary: Reviewed the 4,278-file snapshot of Apache TomEE 7.0.0-SNAPSHOT (Tomcat 8.0.32, CXF 3.1.5, OpenWebBeans 1.6.3; i.e. ~Q1-Q2 2016). I traced remote/EJB/HTTP request handling, deserialization filtering, authentication wrappers, JNDI/deployment, session management, XML/zip/file handling, and the optional SSH/CLI admin module. The snapshot already contains the CVE-2016-0779 mitigation (BlacklistClassResolver applied in both EjbObjectInputStream implementations, ObjectInputStreamFiltered, QuartzObjectInputStream), so that historical issue is not re-exposed in its original form. The strongest single candidate I could substantiate from source is an authentication-bypass in the container's BASIC-auth enforcement wrapper used by the standalone/embedded OpenEJB HTTP registries: GET requests are forwarded to the protected listener even when no credentials were supplied or credentials failed, contradicting the wrapper's purpose and its own "login failed, return 401" branch. Other plausible but weaker leads (path traversal in CLI path resolution, path traversal in embedded resource serving, auto-created default admin credentials, incomplete gadget blacklist) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed because each needs either privileged access, non-default test-only configuration, or is documented/ineffective hardening rather than a demonstrable control failure.
